old: "Use the *pretérito* *perfecto* to talk about recent actions and experiences connected to the present. Review the auxiliary forms *he*, *has*, *ha*, *hemos* and *han* with past participles. Family members can be the subject of the sentence: *Mi madre ha llamado*. *Mis padres han hablado*."
new: "You know the *pretérito* *perfecto* from Unit 1: *he*, *has*, *ha*, *hemos* or *han* plus a past participle. Use it again to talk about recent actions of your family: *Mi madre ha llamado*. *Mis padres han hablado*."

old: "String the five auxiliary forms into one memorable chain: *he*, *has*, *ha*, *hemos*, *han* — the same five endings you would use for any -ar/-er/-ir verb in the present, just borrowed here for *haber*."
new: "Learn the forms as one chain: *he*, *has*, *ha*, *hemos*, *han*. Only the auxiliary changes with the subject; the participle stays the same: *ha llamado*, *han llamado*."
why: False tip: he/has/ha/hemos/han are not "the same five endings" of any -ar/-er/-ir verb.

old: "Use *ya* to say that an action has already happened and *todavía no* to say that it has not happened yet. Both combine naturally with the *pretérito* *perfecto*: *Ya he contestado*. *Todavía no he enviado el mensaje*."

old: "Use the two markers to contrast different family members in the same story: *Ya ha llamado mi madre, pero todavía no ha contestado mi padre* — one subject per clause makes the contrast do the work, with no extra connecting words needed."
new: "Use the two markers to contrast two family members: *Ya ha llamado mi madre, pero todavía no ha contestado mi padre*. Each clause has its own subject and its own marker, and *pero* joins them."
why: The tip says "no extra connecting words needed" but its own example uses pero.
